paper_metadata.title: Acute Diffusion Tensor and Kurtosis Imaging and Outcome following Mild Traumatic Brain Injury

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a large, population-based recruitment strategy from both a level 1 trauma center and a general practitioner clinic, ensuring a representative sample of mixed-mechanism mTBI. Inclusion/exclusion criteria are well-defined, and the control group is matched on key demographics.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: The patients with mTBI were part of the population-based Trondheim mTBI follow-up study (total n = 378), recruited from April 2014 to December 2015 at two emergency departments: a level 1 trauma center in Trondheim, Norway, and at the Trondheim Municipal Emergency clinic
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the geographical and clinical source of the population.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: recruited from April 2014 to December 2015 at two emergency departments: a level 1 trauma center in Trondheim, Norway, and at the Trondheim Municipal Emergency clinic, a general practitioner-run, outpatient clinic.
items.reasoning: Recruitment from both specialized and primary care settings reduces referral bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: recruited from April 2014 to December 2015
items.reasoning: Specific dates are provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Trondheim, Norway... level 1 trauma center... and at the Trondheim Municipal Emergency clinic
items.reasoning: Specific locations and types of facilities are named.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria were age 16 to 59 years and having sustained a TBI, defined as mild per the World Health Organization Collaborating Center Task Force on Mild Traumatic Brain Injury criteria
items.reasoning: Standardized clinical criteria (WHO) and age ranges are used.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: A total of 199 patients participated in an extended follow-up study including acute MRI... 176 of these were assessed for PPCS at 3 months, constituting the study sample (88% of the patients in the extended follow-up).
items.reasoning: The participation rate of 88% from the extended follow-up cohort is high.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1. Participant Characteristics and Injury-Related Factors... Age, Female sex, Education, Vocabulary, Cause of injury, GCS score, LOC, PTA, Complicated mTBI, Level of care
items.reasoning: Comprehensive baseline data is provided in Table 1.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study maintained a high follow-up rate (88%) for the primary outcome. The authors also performed a sensitivity analysis comparing included and excluded participants to check for systematic differences.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 176 of these were assessed for PPCS at 3 months, constituting the study sample (88% of the patients in the extended follow-up).
items.reasoning: An 88% completion rate is well above the standard 80% threshold for low risk.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Differences between included and excluded participants are presented in Table 1 of the Supplementary Material.
items.reasoning: The authors analyzed the characteristics of those lost to follow-up.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: 186 out of the 199 patients in the extended follow-up had DTI and DKI data that passed quality control, and 176 of these were assessed for PPCS at 3 months
items.reasoning: While the flow of participants is clear, specific individual reasons for dropping out of the 3-month assessment (e.g., moved, withdrew consent) are not explicitly detailed in the main text.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Differences between included and excluded participants are presented in Table 1 of the Supplementary Material.
items.reasoning: The authors explicitly state they compared these groups.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The text refers to a supplementary table for these differences but does not summarize the findings of that comparison in the main manuscript.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (DTI/DKI metrics) were measured using standardized 3T MRI protocols within a very tight acute window (72h). The use of TBSS and automated processing limits subjective bias.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Eight diffusion metrics were examined: fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (AD), radial diffusivity (RD), kurtosis fractional anisotropy (KFA), mean kurtosis (Kmean), axial kurtosis (Kax), and radial kurtosis (Krad).
items.reasoning: All metrics are explicitly listed and defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: MRI on a 3T Siemens Skyra system... single-shot balanced-echo EPI sequence acquired in 30 non-collinear directions with 3 b-values
items.reasoning: Standardized high-field MRI and established DTI/DKI sequences were used.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise statistical analysis of the diffusion data was performed using Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS).
items.reasoning: The analysis treats diffusion metrics as continuous variables across the whole brain skeleton.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All analyses were performed with... scanner upgrade... controlled for in all analyses.
items.reasoning: The same scanner was used, and the authors statistically adjusted for a software upgrade.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: A total of 186 out of the 199 patients in the extended follow-up had DTI and DKI data that passed quality control
items.reasoning: 93% of the imaging data was usable.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study appears to use complete-case analysis for the imaging data rather than imputation.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (PPCS) was measured using a validated instrument (BC-PSI) at a standardized time point (3 months). The definition of PPCS is clearly operationalized.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: PPCS was defined as having ≥ 3 core symptoms rated at least moderate (score ≥ 3), or a total score of 13–52
items.reasoning: The threshold for the outcome is explicitly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: PPCS were assessed at 3 months after injury with the British Columbia Postconcussion Symptom Inventory (BC-PSI).
items.reasoning: The BC-PSI is a recognized clinical tool for this purpose.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: PPCS were assessed at 3 months after injury with the British Columbia Postconcussion Symptom Inventory (BC-PSI).
items.reasoning: All patients were assessed at the same interval using the same tool.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study identifies and adjusts for a major confounder (cognitive reserve/vocabulary), which significantly changed the results. However, other potential confounders like pre-injury mental health or litigation status were not included in the multivariable models.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Age, age2, sex, and scanner upgrade... vocabulary scores included as an additional covariate
items.reasoning: Key demographics and cognitive reserve were measured, but pre-existing psychiatric history (a known PPCS risk factor) was not explicitly adjusted for in the TBSS models.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: The Vocabulary subtest from the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence... estimate of preinjury intelligence and a proxy of cognitive reserve
items.reasoning: The proxy for cognitive reserve is well-defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The Vocabulary subtest is considered an estimate of general mental ability and test performance has been shown to be unaffected by cognitive impairment following mTBI.
items.reasoning: The authors justify the reliability of the vocabulary test as a stable pre-injury proxy.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: administered 2 weeks after the injury.
items.reasoning: Standardized timing for the cognitive assessment.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: 10 patients with PPCS, and 9 patients without, had missing vocabulary
items.reasoning: The authors note missing data but do not describe imputation; they likely used listwise deletion for the adjusted models.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Age-, sex-, and education-matched community controls (n = 78)were recruited
items.reasoning: The control group was matched to the patient cohort.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Age, age2, sex, and scanner upgrade (due to scanner upgrade from version D13 to E11 during the inclusion period) were controlled for in all analyses.
items.reasoning: Statistical adjustment was performed for primary demographic and technical variables.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach (TBSS with TFCE and FWE correction) is rigorous and standard for neuroimaging. The authors report both adjusted and unadjusted models, providing transparency regarding the impact of cognitive reserve.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Voxel-wise statistical analysis of the diffusion data was performed using Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS)... non-parametric, permutation-based method using threshold-free cluster enhancement
items.reasoning: The methodology is described in detail.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Because diffusion metrics show a non-linear association with age through adulthood (e.g., FA peaks around the age of 30), both age and age2 were included in all models.
items.reasoning: The inclusion of age-squared shows a biologically informed modeling strategy.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: correction for multiple comparisons (family-wise error rate). A p value of <0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons, was considered statistically significant.
items.reasoning: Stringent correction for multiple comparisons was applied.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2. Comparisons with Significant Findings... Eight diffusion metrics were examined
items.reasoning: The authors report results for all eight metrics across multiple group comparisons and adjustment levels.
